# Advanced modelling: marginalisation, decentring, and new distributions {#sec-advanced}


- The 2027 payoff the whole plan builds toward: graph-rewriting
  features that need the flat registry underneath them, plus the
  new-distribution and module infrastructure. Grouping label: the
  `advanced-features` cluster.
- Marginalisation and decentring *transform the DAG* - replace a
  discrete node with a sum over its support; reparameterise a
  subgraph. Rewriting plain-data records in a flat table is easy;
  rewriting a doubly-linked R6 object graph is not - which is why this
  milestone follows milestone 11.

**The design already exists.** The intended *usage* is in
[#157](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/157) (helpers like
`marginal_poisson()`, a general `marginalise()` syntax); the intended
*mechanism* is in the
[#344](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/pull/344) draft (scalar
discrete variables, and multivariate normals via Laplace
approximation). Both are read-first material for the restart.


## Sprint item: marginalisation

- **this needs no new issue: it is
  [#157](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/157).** #157 already asks
  for both the specific helpers (`marginal_poisson()`) and the general
  `marginalise()` interface, so what follows is design detail *for* #157 rather
  than separate work. It comes from the
  [#322](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/322) sprint plan (§3,
  "Marginalisation"); the draft mechanism is PR
  [#344](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/pull/344), kept open under this
  milestone for the design it records.
- Finish and release the marginalisation interface: integrate discrete
  random variables out of a model, and integrate out *a priori*
  multivariate-normal variables via the Laplace approximation.
- branch intent: PR [#344](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/344) ("An interface for marginalisation of random
  variables … initially just scalar discrete variables, and
  multivariate normal variables via Laplace approximation") on
  `feature/marginalise`. Appendix triage closes the 6-year-stale PR
  but preserves its design; the rebased variants
  (`feature-marginalise-rebased/-squash/-update`) are the restart
  material.
- mechanism: **discrete marginalisation** replaces a discrete latent
  node with an explicit sum over its finite support in the model's
  log-probability - a DAG rewrite. **Laplace marginalisation**
  integrates out *a priori* MVN variables with a Gaussian
  approximation, dropping them from the free state. Both let HMC run
  on a smaller, smoother, fully-continuous parameter space.
- interface ([#157](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/157)): distribution-style helpers such as
  `marginal_poisson()` for the common conjugate/discrete cases, plus a
  general `marginalise()` naming which variables to integrate out.
- finding: both are graph rewrites - delete a node, splice in a sum or
  a Laplace term - which is precisely what the flat node registry
  (milestone 11) makes tractable; rewriting the doubly-linked R6 node
  graph is the blocker today. Depends on milestone 11.
- fix: rebase [#344](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/344)'s mechanism onto the flat registry; implement
  `marginalise()` and the `marginal_*()` helpers; write the
  explanatory documentation (§3.5) that marginalisation needs, since
  it is unfamiliar to most MCMC users.
- priority: medium (2027 headline; needs milestone 11 first).


## Sprint item: sampling discrete variables

- not a GitHub issue - from the [#322](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/322) sprint plan (§4, "Sampling
  discrete variables"). ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Drafted issue body, unfiled

Written but not filed.

*Proposed title: Allow discrete random variables to be sampled, not just observed*

greta's discrete distributions can only ever be *data*. You can write
`distribution(y) <- poisson(lambda)` where `y` is observed, but you cannot make
a Poisson variable a free parameter and have greta sample it.

#### What happens now

`check_unfixed_discrete_distributions()` (`R/checkers.R:1687`), called from
`model()` at `R/greta_model_class.R:97`, walks the DAG and aborts if any
distribution node is discrete and its target is not a data node:

> Model contains a discrete random variable that doesn't have a fixed value, so
> inference cannot be carried out.

That guard is correct given the samplers available. HMC and its variants need a
continuous, differentiable free state, and there is nothing to differentiate
through a discrete support. Nine distributions carry `discrete = TRUE` in
`R/probability_distributions.R`: `bernoulli`, `binomial`, `beta_binomial`,
`poisson`, `negative_binomial`, `hypergeometric`, `dirichlet_multinomial`,
`multinomial` and `categorical`.

#### What it would take

Three pieces, in order:

1. **A latent discrete node.** Let a discrete distribution define a variable
   node rather than only accept a data target, which means relaxing the
   variable and free-state machinery where it assumes continuous support.
2. **A discrete sampler.** A categorical or Metropolis kernel over the discrete
   support, alongside `hmc()` and `adaptive_hmc()`. TFP supplies discrete
   transition kernels to build on.
3. **A Gibbs driver.** Partition the free state into discrete and continuous
   blocks and alternate: HMC on the continuous block given the current discrete
   draw, the discrete kernel on the discrete block given the current continuous
   draw.

#### Relationship to marginalisation

This is the complement of #157. Marginalising a discrete variable integrates it
out so HMC can run on a smaller, smooth space; sampling it keeps it in the model
and gives it a kernel of its own. *Marginalise where you can, sample where you
must.* The two share the same free-state work, so whichever is done first should
expect to carry some of the other's cost.

#### Sequencing

This is a large internals change and it wants the flat node registry
(milestone 11) underneath it — partitioning the free state and swapping kernels
per block means rewriting the graph, which is what the registry work makes
tractable. Doing it against the current doubly-linked R6 node objects is the
blocker today.

#### Acceptance

Validate against discrete-latent posteriors with known answers, using the Geweke
harness (`tests/testthat/test_posteriors_geweke.R`, run with
`GRETA_GEWEKE=true`). A discrete sampler that passes Geweke on a model whose
posterior is known analytically is the bar; anything less and we will not know
whether the kernel is correct.
:::

- Let greta sample discrete random *variables*: discrete latent
  variables, discrete-only samplers, and Gibbs alternation between
  discrete and continuous parameter spaces.
- problem: greta's discrete distributions (`bernoulli`, `binomial`,
  `poisson`, … all carry `discrete = TRUE` in
  `R/probability_distributions.R`) can currently only be *observed
  data* in a likelihood, never free variables - because the
  HMC/leapfrog samplers need a continuous, differentiable free state.
- finding, internals refactor: (1) allow a discrete distribution to
  define a *latent variable* node, relaxing the variable/free-state
  machinery that assumes continuous support; (2) add discrete-only
  samplers - a categorical/Metropolis kernel over the discrete support
  (TFP supplies discrete transition kernels); (3) partition the free
  state into discrete and continuous blocks and Gibbs-alternate: HMC
  on the continuous block given the discrete draw, a discrete kernel
  on the discrete block given the continuous draw. This is the
  internals redesign [#322](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/322) §4 flags, and it rides the same flat-registry
  work as everything else in this milestone (milestone 11).
- relation: the complement to marginalisation above - marginalise
  where you can, sample where you must - so the two sprint items share
  the free-state/registry refactor.
- fix: introduce a discrete free-state partition; add a discrete
  sampler class alongside `hmc()`/`adaptive_hmc()`; implement a Gibbs
  driver composing the two; validate against known discrete-latent
  posteriors with the Geweke harness (milestone 4 aside).
- priority: low-medium (2027; large internals change).


## What this milestone unlocks in 2027

- **Marginalisation and decentring** on the completed registry: the
  graph-rewriting features
  ([#344](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/pull/344),
  [#157](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/157),
  [#47](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/47)).
- **The second backend**: a JAX substrate behind the op dictionary, or
  whichever endgame the fork resolves to.
- **Speed releases**: many chains by default
  ([#294](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/294)),
  tuning-in-backend
  ([#547](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/547)), and the
  representations fast path restored (the 250x on big matrices,
  @sec-cholesky).

## [Issue #345](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/345)

- 2020-02-26
- enhancement
- Bayesian R-squared for a greta model fit.
- problem: there is no way to compute a Bayesian R-squared from a greta fit. The ingredients are available - the response vector, and posterior draws of the linear predictor from `calculate()` - but the user has to assemble them.
- finding: the July 2026 pass recorded this as delivered by greta.checks, where `bayes_R2()` runs correctly against greta 0.6.0 (median 0.216, CI [0.146, 0.286]). That verdict was explicitly **contingent on the greta.checks adoption going ahead**, and it has not. The maintainer's ruling (August 2026) is that [#345](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/345) is not resolved, so it stays open here until the adoption question settles.
- fix: no core greta code if greta.checks is adopted - `bayes_R2()` already exists there and reimplementing it in core greta would duplicate essentially the same formula. If the adoption does not go ahead, implement it against the posterior draws of the linear predictor. Either way the decision, not the code, is what blocks this.
- priority: low, and gated on the greta.checks decision rather than on any work in this milestone.
- defect in the proposed fix: the acceptance test in `fixes/issue-345.md` does not run. It builds on `distribution(as_data(rnorm(10))) <- normal(mu, 1)`, which parses but fails at runtime with *"target of assignment expands to non-language object"* - a replacement function needs an assignable name on the left, so the test fails at model definition, before reaching the behaviour under test. Assign first: `y <- as_data(rnorm(10))`, then `distribution(y) <- normal(mu, 1)`.

It builds on `distribution(as_data(rnorm(10))) <- normal(mu, 1)`, which parses but fails at runtime with *"target of assignment expands to non-language object"* - a replacement function needs an assignable name on the left, so the test fails at model definition, before reaching the behaviour under test. Assign first: `y <- as_data(rnorm(10))`, then `distribution(y) <- normal(mu, 1)`.
